questions.q: Ferro's three business units each run on a separate org today. What does this lesson say about how that multi-org estate most likely came to exist?
options: An architect deliberately chose multi-org for data-residency compliance reasons
The three units were always planned to stay permanently separate by design
Salesforce requires one org per legal entity by policy
It happened because each acquired company kept its existing org rather than being migrated, not from a deliberate architecture decision
questions.explain: The lesson names this directly: Ferro's multi-org estate is an unplanned byproduct of each acquisition keeping its own org, not a deliberate architectural choice that now needs to be defended or undone on its own terms.

questions.q: What real cost does consolidating Ferro's three orgs into one introduce, per this lesson?
options: Each unit's distinct, legitimately different processes now have to be reconciled into shared objects, and one unit's customization risk now has blast radius across the whole org
Consolidation has no real costs, only benefits
Consolidation automatically deletes all historical Opportunity data
Consolidation is only possible if all three units sell identical products
questions.explain: Consolidation isn't free: distinct per-unit processes have to be reconciled onto shared objects, and a single org means one unit's bad automation or deploy can now affect every unit, not just its own — a real tradeoff against the reporting benefit.

questions.q: What does staying multi-org specifically fail to solve, per Ferro's original request?
options: It fails to let each unit use its own sales process
It fails to give Ferro a single combined view of a customer who buys from more than one business unit
It fails to let each unit control its own admin team
It fails to isolate one unit's customization risk from another's
questions.explain: Staying multi-org keeps the exact gap Ferro's leadership wants closed: no single Account record or combined pipeline view for a customer who buys from more than one unit, since that would require joining data across org boundaries.

questions.q: After consolidating to a single org, what does a business-unit field on Account/Opportunity accomplish by itself, with no sharing rule behind it?
options: It replaces the need for organization-wide defaults entirely
It fully restricts each unit's reps to seeing only their own unit's records automatically
It tags records for reporting and filtering, but does nothing on its own to restrict which reps can see which unit's records
It automatically creates a record type for each business unit
questions.explain: A field is just a value for reporting and filtering — it doesn't enforce access on its own. Without a sharing rule (or record type plus sharing rule) keyed off that field, a sufficiently open OWD would let a rep see every unit's records including ones that should stay confidential.

questions.q: What two-part pattern does this lesson say applies at Ferro's larger multi-unit scale, reused from the Harrow sales-org case in Lesson 1?
options: Role hierarchy replaces the need for any business-unit field
Record types alone are sufficient to control both process and visibility
OWD alone can express both the sales process and the visibility rule
A field or record type answers what kind of record/process this is; a sharing mechanism separately answers who can see it
questions.explain: Just as in Lesson 1, process (what a record looks like / which rules it follows) and visibility (who can see it) are two separate questions that need two separate mechanisms — a business-unit field or record type for the first, a sharing rule for the second.
